items.title: Dorothy Tait Interview, 1968-12-21
items.q: The interviewee does not speak in the provided transcript. The mention of 'Ole Miss Simeon' is made by the [INTERVIEWER] in a historical context ('original history... with your giant, with your Johnny Dodds and Ole Miss Simeon').

ctx.x: Um, how do you feel about George in relation to New Orleans jazz, uh, history let's say, and his position? And, um, how do you think people, uh, do you think you'll continue to be acknowledged or do you think you'll be considered greater when you get, when, as time goes on? Or do you think you'll be considered as long or, uh, do you have any sense of, uh, his position?

Yeah, I, I think, uh, you have to divide New Orleans jazz history into two periods. I think the original history and its death, its demise almost completely with your giant, with your Johnny Dodds and Ole Miss Simeon. And then, uh, nothing. And then the revival with George and Bonk. And then George Lewis emerging as really the, the great giant on the clarinet and maintaining this position. And the fact that this music ever got off the old scratchy 78s, I think, is in a large measure George's contribution. And the…

Um, how do you feel about the future of this music in general? I mean, as we know in New Orleans, the younger, younger people in New Orleans really aren't thinking out of music. Um, how do you feel about the future in general? Not necessarily for the rest of it.
